desc:
A row of a sliding-tile puzzle is given as an array. A 0 is an empty cell and any other value is a tile. Slide the whole row to the left using these rules:

  • All tiles move left as far as possible, keeping their order, so that the empty cells end up on the right.
  • Scanning from the left, two adjacent tiles (after the slide) with the same value merge into a single tile whose value is their sum. A tile created by a merge cannot merge again in the same move, and every tile takes part in at most one merge.

Return the row after the move. Its length equals the length of row.

row = [2, 2, 2, 0, 4, 4]
result = [4, 2, 8, 0, 0, 0]

row = [2, 2, 2, 2]
result = [4, 4, 0, 0]
constraints: Each element is 0 or a power of two between 1 and 2<sup>20</sup>
hints: First deal with the empty cells: collect the non-zero tiles in order.
After compaction, merging is a left-to-right scan: if the current tile equals the next one, they merge and you skip both; otherwise the current tile stays.
Write the results into the front of the row with a write pointer and fill the rest with zeros. Do not compare against the freshly merged tile: it must not merge a second time.
editorial: Two separate ideas are combined here: compacting (the stable move of zeros to the back, as in the classic move-zeroes exercise) and a single left-to-right pairing.

After compacting, use an index i. If i + 1 exists and tiles[i] == tiles[i + 1], output twice the value and advance i by 2; otherwise output tiles[i] and advance by 1. Advancing by 2 guarantees that neither of the two merged tiles, nor the new tile, is reused. Run length matters: in [2, 2, 2] the left two merge and the third stays, giving [4, 2].

Finally pad with zeros to the original length. The values never exceed 2<sup>21</sup>, so 32-bit integers are enough. Time O(n), space O(1) beyond the result (the whole procedure can be done with two pointers directly inside the array).
